## 07/10/2026 00:06 — Where OpenClaw Actually Runs

Partner, I found the important question buried in your pasted transcript:

> **Is this OpenClaw/AGENTS/skills idea only for VS Code, or can we use it in this ChatGPT web page, Claude web, Perplexity, etc.?** fileciteturn0file0L1-L1

**No — it is not a VS Code feature.** But there is an important distinction.

### Think of 3 different layers

```text
                     YOUR GOVERNANCE
              AGENTS.md + skills + scripts
                         │
        ┌────────────────┼─────────────────┐
        ▼                ▼                 ▼
   CODING AGENT      OPENCLAW         WEB CHAT
   Claude Code       runtime          ChatGPT
   Codex CLI                          Claude.ai
   Gemini CLI                         Perplexity
        │                │                 │
        ▼                ▼                 ▼
  DIRECTLY reads/    Can load/use      Usually cannot
  executes repo      skills/tools      automatically run
  instructions                         your local repo skills
```

### 1. VS Code — **yes, but VS Code isn't the important part**

Claude Code or Codex can run from a terminal, IDE integration, or other supported environment.

The official shared-skills repo specifically gives installation locations for both:

```text
~/.codex/skills
~/.claude/skills
```

So the same canonical skills can be exposed to **Codex and Claude Code**. citeturn0search1

Therefore:

**VS Code is just the interface.**

The important thing is that the **agent has filesystem + Git + execution access**.

---

### 2. Claude Code — **YES, very applicable**

This is probably the cleanest immediate application for your current development workflow.

Instead of repeatedly sending Claude:

> Follow Git protocol → read tracker → work → test → update artifacts → commit → handoff...

Claude Code gets a canonical skill.

```text
TalkProof Git
│
├── AGENTS.md
│
└── .agents/
    └── skills/
        ├── git-turn/
        ├── implementation/
        ├── testing/
        ├── handoff/
        └── traceability/
```

Claude executes against those rules.

The official OpenClaw shared-skills project explicitly supports symlinking its skills into Claude Code. citeturn0search1

---

### 3. Codex — **YES**

Same principle.

And OpenClaw itself now has a `coding-agent` skill capable of delegating coding work to Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode. citeturn0search2

So:

```text
                 OUR CANONICAL RULES
                       │
                ┌──────┴──────┐
                ▼             ▼
           Claude Code       Codex
                │             │
                └──────┬──────┘
                       ▼
                   TalkProof
```

This is exactly where the approach becomes valuable.

---

### 4. This ChatGPT webpage we're using — **not automatically in the same way**

This distinction matters.

You cannot simply put:

```text
~/.agents/skills/git-turn/SKILL.md
```

on your Windows machine and expect **this ChatGPT browser conversation** to automatically read and execute it.

This ChatGPT session is not your local Claude/Codex process.

Today you compensate for that by telling me:

> follow the Git turn protocol

and having the relevant Git/project environment available through connected capabilities.

So there are really two things:

```text
CHATGPT WEB
   │
   ├── ChatGPT's own tools/capabilities
   ├── connected sources
   ├── conversation instructions/context
   └── project files made available to it

LOCAL CODING AGENT
   │
   ├── filesystem
   ├── Git
   ├── AGENTS.md
   ├── SKILL.md
   ├── scripts
   └── shell/test execution
```

They're not equivalent.

---

### 5. Claude.ai webpage — **same limitation**

Don't confuse:

**Claude.ai chat**

with

**Claude Code**.

```text
Claude.ai web chat
        ≠
Claude Code
```

Claude Code is designed to work directly with repositories, files, shell commands, agent instructions and skills.

A normal Claude web conversation doesn't automatically inherit an arbitrary local `~/.claude/skills` directory just because it exists on your PC.

---

### 6. Perplexity — **not directly**

Again, you can give Perplexity a document containing the methodology and ask it to follow it.

But that's different from:

```text
skill detected
      ↓
skill loaded
      ↓
script executed
      ↓
Git inspected
      ↓
validator executed
      ↓
failure blocks completion
```

For our purpose I'd treat Perplexity primarily as **research**, not as an execution participant in this engineering governance loop.

---

# OpenClaw itself is another possibility

This is where your question becomes more interesting.

OpenClaw isn't simply a collection of files.

It is an **agent runtime/gateway**. Its current quick-start documentation says it can reuse existing Claude Code/Codex authentication and opens a web dashboard after configuration. citeturn0search4

And OpenClaw can run external coding harnesses including **Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI and others** through its agent infrastructure. citeturn0search11

So theoretically:

```text
                       YOU
                        │
                  OPENCLAW
                        │
             ┌──────────┼───────────┐
             ▼          ▼           ▼
           Claude      Codex      Gemini
            Code
             │          │           │
             └──────────┼───────────┘
                        ▼
                     Git repo
                        │
                skills + validators
```

That is much closer to the reel's promise.

---

# But I wouldn't install OpenClaw yet

This is the important decision.

You **don't need OpenClaw to obtain the most valuable benefit**.

The shared skills repository itself says its goal is:

> write the workflow once and reuse it everywhere.

And supports Claude Code + Codex directly. citeturn0search1

So I'd test this in stages:

| Stage | What we test | Risk |
|---|---|---:|
| **1** | `AGENTS.md` | Very low |
| **2** | One `git-turn` skill | Low |
| **3** | Claude Code reads it | Low |
| **4** | Codex reads same canonical skill | Low |
| **5** | Add validator | Low |
| **6** | Test TalkProof workflow | Medium |
| **7** | Only then evaluate OpenClaw runtime | Separate decision |

That avoids introducing another giant tool before proving the underlying idea.

---

# And this connects to another reel in your transcript

You pasted another claim about huge contexts causing quality problems — “context rot” / lost-in-the-middle — and using external structure rather than continuously dumping everything into the context window. fileciteturn0file0L1-L1

**That is directly relevant here.**

Our current approach sometimes becomes:

```text
NEW PAGE

"Here is previous handover..."
+ protocol
+ tracker
+ specifications
+ review
+ old decisions
+ Claude output
+ more instructions
+ another prompt
+ DON'T FORGET X
+ DON'T FORGET Y

             ↓

       HUGE CONTEXT
```

Skills permit a different architecture:

```text
                 SMALL ACTIVE CONTEXT
                         │
                "Review WP-17"
                         │
                         ▼
                  Agent discovers
                         │
           ┌─────────────┼────────────┐
           ▼             ▼            ▼
       git-turn      review-skill    D-scale
           │             │            │
           └─────────────┼────────────┘
                         ▼
                  fetch only needed
                  repo evidence
                         │
                         ▼
                      reason
```

**That may be a bigger benefit than token savings.**

It reduces the amount of operational procedure competing with the actual engineering problem for the model's attention.

---

# One correction to my previous answer

After checking the current OpenClaw docs more deeply, OpenClaw's skill system has evolved beyond simply `skills/`.

It now has multiple levels of skill loading, including workspace, project/personal and managed skills, with explicit precedence rules. citeturn0search0turn0search6

That's actually useful for us because we could eventually have:

```text
GLOBAL — YOUR ENGINEERING OS
────────────────────────────
git-turn
evidence-rules
no-false-completion
handoff
audit

             +

TALKPROOF-SPECIFIC
────────────────────────────
D-scale
TalkProof architecture
TalkProof test gates
TalkProof traceability

             +

TASK-SPECIFIC
────────────────────────────
WP-17
```

That is much cleaner than copying one giant protocol into every project.

## My recommendation

**Don't “adopt OpenClaw.”**

First extract the architectural idea and run a controlled experiment on **one tiny part of TalkProof**:

> **Can Claude Code and Codex follow exactly the same Git-turn skill, with a validator detecting when either agent fails to comply?**

If **yes**, then we have proven something valuable: a large part of the manual governance work you've been doing in these chats can move from **prompt reminders → executable engineering infrastructure**.

Only after that test would I decide whether OpenClaw itself adds enough value to justify another runtime. memcite

## 06/10/2026 23:53 — Viral OpenClaw Claim Check

Partner, **the reel is based on something real, but it badly mangles the name and exaggerates what was released.**

The person is **Peter Steinberger**, not “Vitas Steinberger.” He is the creator/lead behind urlOpenClawhttps://github.com/openclaw/openclaw. The current OpenClaw material explicitly credits “Peter Steinberger and the community.” citeturn0search2

More importantly for **what we have been doing with TalkProof/Git/turn protocols**, there really is something worth studying here.

### What is actually true

The official OpenClaw organization has published an open-source repository called urlOpenClaw Agent Skillshttps://github.com/openclaw/agent-skills. It describes itself as the **public canonical source for common agent workflows**. citeturn0search1

It contains the architecture the reel is talking about:

```text
agent-skills/
├── AGENTS.md
├── skills/
│   ├── agent-transcript/
│   ├── autoreview/
│   ├── behavior-validator/
│   ├── beam/
│   ├── crabbox/
│   ├── handoff/
│   └── session-viewer/
└── scripts/
    ├── install-skills
    ├── validate-skills
    └── check-skills
```

And **Codex + Claude Code sharing the same skills is explicitly supported**. The repo gives installation/symlink instructions for both `~/.codex/skills` and `~/.claude/skills`. citeturn0search1

So this part of the reel is substantially correct:

**write the operating procedure once → make multiple coding agents consume the same procedure.**

---

### But the reel oversells several things

| Reel claim | What I can verify |
|---|---|
| “Vitas Steinberger” created OpenClaw | ❌ Wrong name. **Peter Steinberger** |
| “He open-sourced his entire personal agent setup” | ⚠️ I cannot substantiate **entire personal setup** |
| Master `AGENTS.md` | ✅ Real |
| Reusable `skills/` | ✅ Real |
| Skills shared with Codex + Claude Code | ✅ Explicitly supported |
| Skill validation scripts | ✅ Real |
| Browser automation | ✅ OpenClaw has browser/tool capabilities |
| WhatsApp/Slack/Discord/iMessage integration | ✅ OpenClaw supports messaging-channel integrations |
| “These skills crawl all his Slack/Discord/WhatsApp/iMessage” | ⚠️ Much stronger claim than the evidence I found |
| “Exact file he personally uses across every project” | ⚠️ I haven't found evidence establishing that |

OpenClaw itself uses workspace files such as `AGENTS.md`, `SOUL.md` and `TOOLS.md`, and workspace skills live under the workspace's `skills/.../SKILL.md`. citeturn0search2turn0search3

There is also an important security point missing from the reel: OpenClaw's own documentation says to treat third-party skills as **untrusted code** and inspect them before enabling them. citeturn0search3

## Why I think this matters to **our** work

This is actually very close to the problem you've repeatedly been solving manually with me and Claude.

For TalkProof, you've been saying things like:

```text
Follow Git turn protocol
↓
Read handover
↓
Read tracker
↓
Do the work
↓
Create review artifact
↓
Update tracker
↓
Commit
↓
Give Claude the handoff
↓
Next turn: DON'T FORGET THE PROTOCOL
```

The architectural idea behind `AGENTS.md + SKILL.md + validators` is:

```text
                 ONE VERSIONED OPERATING SYSTEM
                           │
                     AGENTS.md
                           │
              ┌────────────┼────────────┐
              ▼            ▼            ▼
          Git Skill    Review Skill   Handoff Skill
              │            │            │
              └────────────┼────────────┘
                           ▼
                    Validation scripts
                           │
             ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
             ▼                           ▼
        Claude Code                    Codex
             │                           │
             └──────── SAME RULES ───────┘
```

And **that is not social-media fantasy**. The official agent-skills repository specifically says its purpose is to write a workflow once and reuse it rather than hand-copying long `SKILL.md` files between repositories. citeturn0search1

### The particularly interesting bit for you

Their root OpenClaw `AGENTS.md` begins with an instruction that the agent must read the root policy and the nearest scoped `AGENTS.md` before working in a subtree, and tells the agent to inspect Git status before editing. citeturn0search4

That is remarkably close to the direction you've independently been pushing:

**Git isn't merely storing the code. Git stores the operating contract for the AI doing the work.**

So I would **not copy Peter's setup wholesale**.

I would study it and compare it against your current TalkProof Git-turn protocol. We may find that a substantial amount of your repeated prompting can become:

**AGENTS.md → reusable skills → deterministic scripts → validators → agent-specific execution.**

That could be a meaningful improvement to the system you've already built, rather than replacing it with OpenClaw. memcite

## 07/10/2026 00:28 — Yes, Claude Web Can Use It

**Yes. Your screenshot proves an important correction to what I said earlier.** I was too restrictive when I said Claude web could not use these skills in the same way.

What you're showing is **Claude.ai → Customize → Skills → Add → Upload skill / Create a skill / Create with Claude**.

Anthropic's current documentation confirms that **custom Skills work directly in Claude.ai chat**, not only Claude Code. You can upload a ZIP containing `skill.md`, enable it, and Claude dynamically loads it when relevant. Skills are currently available on Free, Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise, provided code execution is enabled. citeturn0search0turn0search3

### This changes our TalkProof idea considerably

We could create:

```text
talkproof-git-turn/
│
├── skill.md
│
├── references/
│   └── turn-protocol.md
│
└── scripts/
    └── validate-turn.py
```

Upload it using exactly the **Upload skill** button you're showing.

Then in a completely new Claude web chat you could say:

> Review the next TalkProof work package.

Claude can identify that the TalkProof Git-turn skill is relevant and load it. Anthropic specifically describes this as **progressive disclosure**: Claude sees enough metadata to identify the relevant skill and loads the detailed material when required rather than putting every skill's complete contents into every context. citeturn0search6

So this can reduce your repeated:

```text
Don't forget Git turn protocol
Don't forget artifact
Don't forget tracker
Don't forget handoff
Don't forget...
```

**even in Claude web.**

And there is an extra benefit I didn't mention: current Claude Code can sync skills from your Claude.ai account. Anthropic says the sync happens when a Claude Code session starts and checks for changes roughly every ten minutes. citeturn0search0

So potentially:

```text
                ONE TALKPROOF SKILL
                        │
                Claude.ai account
                        │
              ┌─────────┴─────────┐
              ▼                   ▼
         CLAUDE WEB           CLAUDE CODE
              │                   │
              └─────────┬─────────┘
                        ▼
              SAME TURN PROTOCOL
```

That's **very relevant to what you're trying to achieve.**

---

# And what about ChatGPT?

Here is the bigger correction:

## **ChatGPT now has Skills too.**

OpenAI's current documentation describes essentially the same concept: reusable workflows, generally defined with a `SKILL.md`, which ChatGPT can automatically select or which the user can explicitly invoke. citeturn0search1turn0search2

The important catch is **account availability**.

OpenAI currently documents ChatGPT Skills as available to eligible **Business, Enterprise, Healthcare and Edu** workspaces. citeturn0search2

So on your current **personal ChatGPT Plus account**, you should **not expect the Claude-like Skills UI to be available**.

When available, the documented ChatGPT route is:

**Sidebar → Plugins → Plugin Directory → Skills**

and users can create through chat/editor or upload a skill from the computer. citeturn0search2

---

# This makes your original idea much more interesting

There's now an emerging **Agent Skills open standard**.

Anthropic says its Agent Skills specification is an open standard and skills aren't inherently locked to Claude. citeturn0search6

OpenAI likewise says its skills are compatible with the **open Agent Skills standard**. citeturn0search8

So instead of designing:

```text
CLAUDE TURN PROTOCOL
+
CHATGPT TURN PROTOCOL
+
CODEX TURN PROTOCOL
+
OPENCLAW TURN PROTOCOL
```

we should investigate designing:

```text
               AUMNITY / YOUR AI OPERATING SYSTEM

                       AGENT SKILLS
                           │
                    ┌──────┴──────┐
                    │  SKILL.md   │
                    │ references  │
                    │ scripts     │
                    └──────┬──────┘
                           │
          ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
          ▼                ▼                ▼
      Claude.ai          Codex           ChatGPT*
          │                │                │
      Claude Code          │            Workspaces*
          │                │
          └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                           ▼
                    SAME GOVERNANCE
```

`*` subject to ChatGPT product/workspace availability.

This is **not just an OpenClaw trick anymore**.

---

## One major warning

A skill gives the model **procedure**.

It does **not magically give every environment identical capabilities**.

For example, our skill might say:

```text
1. git status
2. read tracker
3. inspect last commit
4. perform review
5. run tests
6. create artifact
7. update tracker
8. commit artifact
```

Claude Code with repository/shell access could execute all of that.

Claude web can understand and follow the same workflow, but whether it can perform each operation depends on the tools/connectors/environment available in that Claude session.

Likewise, a ChatGPT skill doesn't magically give ChatGPT access to a Git repository. OpenAI describes the same separation: **skills provide the workflow; tools/plugins provide live information and actions.** citeturn0search9

So:

```text
SKILL = HOW I WANT THE AI TO WORK

TOOLS = WHAT THE AI IS ACTUALLY ABLE TO DO
```

That's the key distinction.

---

# This is worth testing — before OpenClaw

I would change my recommendation based on what you've shown me.

**Don't install OpenClaw first.**

First create **one portable Agent Skill** from the Git-turn protocol you've already developed through all these TalkProof sessions.

Then test exactly the same skill in:

| Environment | Test |
|---|---|
| Claude.ai | Does it automatically follow our turn protocol? |
| Claude Code | Does it execute the protocol against Git? |
| Codex | Can the same/open-standard skill work? |
| ChatGPT Plus | Not currently the documented Skills target |
| ChatGPT eligible workspace | Test same skill when available |
| OpenClaw | **Only later**, if it adds orchestration we actually need |

If that succeeds, we've found something much more significant than the viral reel:

**Your months of accumulated AI-working rules can become a portable, versioned AI operating system instead of instructions you repeatedly type into individual chats.**

And *that* directly attacks one of the biggest problems you've been experiencing across TalkProof: Claude and ChatGPT forgetting or drifting from the process between pages/turns. memcite

## 06/10/2026 23:56 — OpenClaw Setup Study

Yes. I studied the actual repositories/docs rather than the reel description.

**There is something genuinely useful here for us.** But I would **not adopt OpenClaw itself yet**. The valuable part is the **operating pattern**.

### What they have actually built

The public urlOpenClaw Agent Skills repositoryhttps://github.com/openclaw/agent-skills describes its purpose very clearly: **write a workflow once, reuse it everywhere, rather than copying long instructions between repositories.** It currently includes reusable skills for review, handoff, behavioural validation, session provenance and remote validation. citeturn0search4turn0search3

The architecture is roughly:

```text
                    SHARED AI OPERATING RULES
                           AGENTS.md
                               │
              ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
              │                │                │
           SKILLS          SCRIPTS         VALIDATORS
              │                │                │
       ┌──────┼──────┐         │                │
       │      │      │         │                │
     Review Handoff Behaviour  deterministic   check
                    Validator  operations      skills
       │      │      │
       └──────┼──────┘
              │
      ┌───────┴────────┐
      ▼                ▼
 Claude Code          Codex
      │                │
      └──── same workflows ────┘
```

Their installer explicitly supports putting the same skill library into both Codex and Claude Code. citeturn0search4

---

# Now compare that with what **we are doing**

This is where it becomes interesting.

You currently have something conceptually like:

```text
TalkProof
│
├── Product specs
├── Sprint tracker
├── Traceability
├── Code
│
├── ChatGPT review instructions
├── Claude implementation instructions
│
├── Git Turn Protocol
│      ├── bootstrap
│      ├── inspect git
│      ├── work
│      ├── test
│      ├── artifact
│      ├── tracker update
│      ├── commit
│      └── handoff
│
└── Hundreds of session/review/handover artifacts
```

The weakness is **not the process itself**.

The weakness is that we're still repeatedly telling agents:

> “Follow turn protocol.”

> “Don't forget Git.”

> “Create the review artifact.”

> “Update tracker.”

> “Give prompt to Claude.”

> “Did you create the artifact for this turn?”

You've had to become the **runtime enforcing the AI runtime**.

That shouldn't be your job.

---

# What I would take from OpenClaw

I would restructure our AI engineering layer like this:

```text
TalkProof repo
│
├── AGENTS.md                    ← constitution
│
├── .agents/
│   │
│   ├── skills/
│   │   │
│   │   ├── git-turn/
│   │   │   └── SKILL.md
│   │   │
│   │   ├── independent-review/
│   │   │   └── SKILL.md
│   │   │
│   │   ├── sprint-closeout/
│   │   │   └── SKILL.md
│   │   │
│   │   ├── handoff/
│   │   │   └── SKILL.md
│   │   │
│   │   ├── traceability/
│   │   │   └── SKILL.md
│   │   │
│   │   └── product-owner-gate/
│   │       └── SKILL.md
│   │
│   └── scripts/
│       ├── validate-turn.py
│       ├── validate-tracker.py
│       ├── validate-handoff.py
│       └── validate-traceability.py
│
├── docs/
├── backend/
├── admin/
└── flutter/
```

That is much closer to a proper **AI development operating system**.

OpenClaw itself supports workspace and project-agent skills and has explicit precedence rules for them. citeturn0search0turn0search1

---

## `AGENTS.md` should NOT contain everything

This is an important lesson from their design.

Don't make a 2,000-line monster saying everything an AI might ever need.

`AGENTS.md` becomes the **constitution**:

```text
# TalkProof Agent Constitution

1. Git is authoritative.
2. Never claim implementation without code evidence.
3. Never claim test success without executable evidence.
4. Read current tracker before changing product state.
5. Preserve traceability.
6. Every engineering turn follows git-turn.
7. Implementation and independent review remain separate.
8. Product-owner blocked decisions cannot be silently assumed.
9. Never hide failures.
10. Every completed unit leaves a reproducible handoff.
```

Then detailed procedures move into skills.

That matches OpenClaw's philosophy: skill bodies are supposed to be **operational and terse**, while reusable command logic belongs in helper scripts. citeturn0search3turn0search4

---

# Example: our Git Turn Protocol becomes a skill

Instead of you reminding me 15 times:

```text
.agents/skills/git-turn/SKILL.md
```

Conceptually:

```text
---
name: git-turn
description: Mandatory engineering-turn lifecycle.
---

BEFORE WORK

1. git status
2. identify branch
3. identify current commit
4. read AGENTS.md
5. read active tracker
6. read previous handoff
7. establish intended work unit

WORK

8. perform only declared work
9. record assumptions
10. record failures
11. run relevant tests

AFTER WORK

12. update evidence
13. update traceability if affected
14. update sprint tracker if affected
15. create turn artifact
16. validate artifact
17. git diff
18. commit
19. verify clean/expected working tree
20. produce next-agent handoff
```

Now Claude doesn't need a giant prompt explaining this.

Codex doesn't need another version.

And theoretically ChatGPT/other agents don't need yet another version.

**One source of truth.**

---

# But OpenClaw has something even more important

### Validators.

This is the piece I think we should steal aggressively.

Currently we depend too much on the model saying:

> “Yes, I followed the protocol.”

That's weak.

Instead:

```text
AI says
"I completed WP-17."
       │
       ▼
validate-turn.py
       │
       ├── artifact exists? ───────── NO → FAIL
       │
       ├── tracker updated? ───────── NO → FAIL
       │
       ├── tests recorded? ────────── NO → FAIL
       │
       ├── evidence referenced? ───── NO → FAIL
       │
       ├── handoff created? ───────── NO → FAIL
       │
       └── Git state acceptable? ──── NO → FAIL
                                      │
                                      ▼
                              TURN NOT COMPLETE
```

OpenClaw's shared repository does exactly this kind of separation: `validate-skills` performs lightweight frontmatter validation, while `check-skills` runs broader syntax/tests/typechecking. citeturn0search4

**This is much stronger than prompt engineering.**

We're moving from:

**“AI, please remember the rules.”**

to:

**“Software prevents the AI from claiming completion unless the rules pass.”**

---

# Their `behavior-validator` is especially relevant to TalkProof

This caught my attention.

Their shared library includes a **behavior-validator**, described as source-blind validation of user-visible behaviour against a contract. citeturn0search4

That's conceptually close to the problem we've repeatedly encountered:

```text
Tracker says DONE
        ≠
Code exists
        ≠
Code integrated
        ≠
Feature works
        ≠
User-visible behaviour works
```

Remember our TalkProof D0–D5 discussion?

We could formalise that:

```text
Requirement
    ↓
Implementation evidence
    ↓
Integration evidence
    ↓
Automated test evidence
    ↓
Behaviour validation
    ↓
Runtime evidence
    ↓
D-level
```

That could make your **D-scale executable rather than merely documented**.

---

# Another useful idea: skills aren't capabilities

OpenClaw explicitly distinguishes these.

A skill is essentially **instructions telling an agent how to use capabilities it already has**. Plugins/tools provide actual capability. citeturn0search10

So:

```text
SKILL
"How TalkProof review must be performed"

≠

TOOL
"Ability to execute Git / browser / database / API"
```

That's an important architectural separation for what you've been building.

---

# Browser claim from the reel

This part is real too.

There is currently a dedicated `browser-automation` skill for multi-step browser control, including checking browser state and recovering from stale references/timeouts. citeturn0search5

But again:

**skill ≠ magical browser.**

The browser plugin/tool provides the capability; the skill tells the agent how to operate it reliably.

---

# One thing I would NOT copy

OpenClaw can discover/load lots of skills automatically.

For our engineering environment, I'd be more restrictive.

OpenClaw itself supports **agent allowlists**, including giving an agent only a specific final set of skills or even none. citeturn0search1

For TalkProof I'd want:

```text
Claude BUILD agent
────────────────────
git-turn
implementation
testing
handoff
traceability

ChatGPT REVIEW agent
────────────────────
git-turn
independent-review
evidence-validation
D-scale
traceability
handoff

PO / Human
────────────────────
product-decision
scope-approval
release-gate
```

Claude shouldn't casually become its own independent reviewer.

Reviewer shouldn't silently become builder.

That's stronger than simply giving every AI every skill.

---

# And there is now a self-improvement concept

OpenClaw has a **Skill Workshop** where an agent can propose reusable work as a new skill rather than immediately altering the canonical skill library. Those proposals can be inspected/evaluated/applied. citeturn0search1

That suggests a very good model for us:

```text
Repeated problem occurs
       ↓
Agent notices pattern
       ↓
PROPOSE new skill/change
       ↓
Human / validator review
       ↓
Accept?
   │          │
  NO         YES
   │          │
 discard     update canonical skill
                 ↓
          all future agents
          inherit improvement
```

That's **learn → fix the operating system → don't repeat the mistake**.

Very close to what you were discussing earlier today about **learn → unlearn → relearn**, except implemented technically.

---

# So where are we compared with this?

My assessment:

| Area | Our current method | OpenClaw pattern | Better direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Git discipline | **Strong** | Strong | Keep ours |
| Turn audit trail | **Very strong** | Some similar mechanisms | Keep ours |
| Product traceability | **Strong** | Not its core purpose | Keep ours |
| Independent review | **Strong concept** | Reusable review skill | Combine |
| Repeated prompts | ❌ Too much | **Much better** | Adopt skills |
| Cross-agent consistency | ⚠️ Manual | **Strong** | Adopt |
| Protocol validation | ⚠️ Mostly AI/human | **Scripts** | Adopt aggressively |
| Skill reuse | ⚠️ Limited | **Excellent** | Adopt |
| Human reminders | ❌ Too many | Reduced | Automate |
| Evidence maturity/D-scale | **Ours is richer** | Behaviour validation useful | Combine |
| Self-improving procedure | Mostly manual | Workshop/proposal model | Adopt later |

### Therefore I would **not replace our system with OpenClaw**.

I would build:

> **Our Git-first engineering governance + OpenClaw-style reusable skills + deterministic validators.**

That is materially better than either approach alone.

And the biggest immediate win isn't WhatsApp, browser automation, or OpenClaw itself.

It's much simpler:

**You should stop having to tell Claude/ChatGPT “don't forget the turn protocol.”**

The protocol should become **machine-enforced infrastructure**. memcite

**`git-turn-governance`**

> bootstrap → establish Git state → read authoritative sources → declare work unit → execute → test → record evidence/failures → update tracker/traceability where applicable → create turn artifact → validate → commit → handoff.

Then we install/test the **same conceptual skill in ChatGPT and Claude**.

The useful test is:

> **Start a fresh conversation, give only a normal TalkProof task, and see whether each AI autonomously invokes the skill and follows the protocol without you saying “don't forget Git turn protocol.”**

Then deliberately create failure cases—missing artifact, uncommitted change, missing tracker update—and see whether the skill/validator catches them.

If that works, **then** we expand into `independent-review`, `D-scale`, `handoff`, `traceability`, etc.

That would give us evidence rather than another architecture idea.

**I think this experiment is worth doing before any further OpenClaw work.** memcite
